source_text: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἐσμὲν ἄθεοι· πρὸς ἓν ἕκαστον ἀπαντήσω τῶν ἐγκλημάτων, μὴ καὶ γελοῖον ᾖ τοὺς λέγοντας μὴ ἐλέγχειν· Διαγόρᾳ μὲν γὰρ εἰκότως ἀθεότητα ἐπεκάλουν Ἀθηναῖοι, μὴ μόνον τὸν Ὀρφικὸν εἰς μέσον κατατιθέντι λόγον καὶ τὰ ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι καὶ τὰ τῶν Καβείρων δημεύοντι μυστήρια καὶ τὸ τοῦ Ἡρακλέους ἵνα τὰς γογγύλας ἑψοῖ κατακόπτοντι ξόανον, ἄντικρυς δὲ ἀποφαινομένῳ μηδ᾿ ὅλως εἶναι θεόν. Ἡμῖν δέ, διαιροῦσιν ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης τὸν θεόν, καὶ δεικνύουσιν ἕτερον μέν τι εἶναι τὴν ὕλην ἄλλο δὲ τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸ διὰ μέσου πολύ (τὸ μὲν γὰρ θεῖον ἀγένητον εἶναι καὶ ἀΐδιον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ θεωρούμενον, τὴν δὲ ὕλην γενητὴν καὶ φθαρτήν), μή τι οὐκ ἀλόγως τὸ τῆς ἀθεότητος ἐπικαλοῦσιν ὄνομα; Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐφρονοῦμεν ὅμοια τῷ Διαγόρᾳ, τοσαῦτα ἔχοντες πρὸς θεοσέβειαν ἐνέχυρα, τὸ εὔτακτον, τὸ διὰ παντὸς σύμφωνον, τὸ μέγεθος, τὴν χροίαν, τὸ σχῆμα, τὴν διάθεσιν τοῦ κόσμου, εἰκότως ἂν ἡμῖν καὶ ἡ τοῦ μὴ θεοσεβεῖν δόξα καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἐλαύνεσθαι αἰτία προσετρίβετο. Ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν ἕνα θεὸν ἄγει τὸν τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ποιητήν, αὐτὸν μὲν οὐ γενόμενον (ὅτι τὸ ὂν οὐ γίνεται ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ ὄν), πάντα δὲ διὰ τοῦ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγου πεποιηκότα, ἑκάτερα ἀλόγως πάσχομεν, καὶ κακῶς ἀγορευόμεθα καὶ διωκόμεθα.
pass_a_gloss: That therefore we are not atheists, to each of the accusations I will respond, lest it be laughable that those speaking do not refute; for to Diagoras indeed the Athenians reasonably charged atheism, not only because he brought into the middle the Orphic account and plundered the mysteries in Eleusis and those of the Cabiri and the wooden image of Heracles in order that he might boil the gourds, but also because he declared outright that god does not exist at all. But to us, who separate God from matter and show that matter is one thing and God is another and that the difference between them is great (for the divine is uncreated and eternal, perceived by mind and reason alone, but matter is created and perishable), do they not unreasonably call us by the name of atheism? For if we thought similarly to Diagoras, having so many pledges of piety, the order, the harmony throughout, the size, the color, the shape, the disposition of the world, it would be reasonable that also the opinion of not being pious and the cause of being despised would be turned against us. But since our reason introduces one God, the creator of this whole universe, who himself has not come into being (because what exists does not come into being, but what does not exist), but has made all things through the reason that comes from him, we suffer both unreasonably and are spoken of badly and persecuted.
pass_b_english: We are not atheists; I will answer each charge so that it does not become laughable for our accusers to leave us unrefuted. The Athenians reasonably charged Diagoras with atheism, not only because he publicly recited the Orphic account, plundered the mysteries of Eleusis and the Cabiri, and chopped up a wooden statue of Heracles to boil his gourds, but also because he declared outright that no god exists at all. Yet we distinguish God from matter, showing that matter is one thing and God another, with a great gulf between them: the divine is uncreated and eternal, perceived only by mind and reason, while matter is created and perishable. Is it not unreasonable, then, for them to pin the label of atheism on us? If we thought like Diagoras, despite possessing such abundant pledges of piety — the world's order, its universal harmony, its size, color, shape, and disposition — it would be fitting for the charge of impiety and the cause of our contempt to stick. But our reason presents one God as the maker of this entire universe, a God who has not come into being (since what truly exists does not become, but what does not exist does), and who made all things through the reason that proceeds from him. For this we suffer unreasonably, are slandered, and are persecuted.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the philosophical distinction between the uncreated divine and created matter, the specific historical references to Diagoras, and the ontological argument regarding existence and becoming. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source.
